entry.title: Understanding memorization and knowledge acquisition in LLMs

link.title: Understanding memorization and knowledge acquisition in LLMs

entry.content:
Introduction

How do Large Language Models (LLMs) acquire factual knowledge during their pretraining phase? This fundamental question lies at the heart of understanding both the capabilities and limitations of modern AI systems. This blog explores the mechanisms of knowledge acquisition and memorization in LLMs, drawing primarily from the groundbreaking study by Chang et al. (NeurIPS 2024): “How do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?”

Background: How are LLMs Trained?

Modern LLMs like GPT, Llama, OLMo, and Mistral follow a decoder-based transformer architecture. The training process consists of several distinct phases:

Training Phases

  1. Pretraining (Next Token Prediction - NTP): ~3 trillion tokens
  2. Supervised Fine-Tuning: ~millions of instruction-response pairs
  3. Alignment with Human Preferences: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) or DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)

What is Next Token Prediction?

The fundamental training objective is simple yet powerful: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next token. This is formalized as minimizing the negative log-likelihood:

L = -Σ log P(x_t | x_<t)

Example: “The Eiffel Tower is located in __”

  • Model learns: P("Paris" | context) should be high
  • Model learns: P("London" | context) should be low

The Optimization Process

For each minibatch:

  1. Forward pass: compute predictions
  2. Compute loss (cross-entropy)
  3. Backward pass: compute gradients
  4. Update weights: θ ← θ - η∇L

This process repeats for billions of examples, with each gradient step slightly adjusting the model’s parameters.

The Core Research Question

How exactly do LLMs acquire factual knowledge during this pretraining process?

Key questions include:

  • Does knowledge acquisition happen gradually or suddenly?
  • How quickly do models forget newly learned facts?
  • Does training on more data improve the ability to learn new facts?
  • How do model size and training stage affect knowledge acquisition?

Methodology: The Fictional Knowledge Experiment

Chang et al. designed an elegant experiment to study knowledge acquisition in controlled conditions.

Creating Fictional Knowledge

They created a fictional world on Mars with:

  • Entities: Zorgon (leader), Calidus government, Mariner Valleys
  • Relations: “leader of”, “government type”, “location of”
  • Facts: “Mars underwent reform under Zorgon’s leadership”

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/kaist-ai/fictional-knowledge

  • 130 training inputs
  • ~1,800 evaluation probes

Model: OLMo

They used OLMo (Open Language Model) in two sizes:

  • OLMo-1B (1 billion parameters)
  • OLMo-7B (7 billion parameters)

At three training checkpoints:

  • Early: 170B tokens processed
  • Mid: 500B tokens processed
  • Late: 1.5T tokens processed

Three Injection Scenarios

  1. Once: Inject fictional knowledge once, then continue normal pretraining
  2. Duplicate: Inject identical text 10 times (every 100 steps)
  3. Paraphrase: Inject paraphrased versions 10 times (every 100 steps)

Three Probe Types

Type Description Example
Memorization Exact sequence recall “Mars underwent reform under Zorgon’s leadership”
Semantic Paraphrased understanding “Mars experienced transformation during Zorgon’s leadership”
Compositional Multi-hop reasoning “The Zorgon-Calidus government expedited democratic transition”

Evaluation Metrics

Acquisition: How well does the model learn the fact initially?

logprob(q|p) where p = context, q = target fact

Retention: How well does the model retain the fact over time?

R(q,t) = [ℓ(q;θ_t) - ℓ(q;θ_pre)] / [ℓ(q;θ_max) - ℓ(q;θ_pre)]

Where:

  • θ_pre: model before injection
  • θ_max: model immediately after injection
  • θ_t: model at t steps after injection

Effectivity: Learning efficiency per exposure

E = Average acquisition across all probes

Key Findings

Finding 1: Knowledge is Acquired Incrementally

Knowledge acquisition occurs through small, cumulative probability increases with each gradient step.

Key observations:

  • Not sudden: Knowledge doesn’t “click” in a single step
  • Sequential improvement: Probability increases gradually across multiple exposures
  • Immediate forgetting: Forgetting begins immediately after acquisition

The model’s confidence in a fact increases with each exposure, but the effect is small and degrades quickly.

Finding 2: Exact Memorization > Semantic Understanding

Across all scenarios:

  • Memorization probes consistently outperform semantic probes
  • Compositional understanding is the most difficult
  • Gap between memorization and semantic understanding persists

This suggests models primarily learn surface patterns rather than deep semantic relationships.

Finding 3: Training Stage Doesn’t Improve Learning Ability

Surprising result: Models don’t get “better” at learning new facts with more pretraining!

Effectivity across training stages (OLMo-7B):

  • Early (170B tokens): E ≈ 0.5
  • Mid (500B tokens): E ≈ 0.5
  • Late (1.5T tokens): E ≈ 0.5

Implication: More training data ≠ better learning capability for new facts

Finding 4: Model Size Matters

Larger models show consistently better acquisition:

  • OLMo-1B: E ≈ 0.3
  • OLMo-7B: E ≈ 0.5

Interpretation: Larger models have higher effectivity per exposure, but this is a constant factor improvement, not exponential.

Finding 5: Duplication vs Paraphrase Trade-offs

Duplication:

  • ✅ Better initial memorization
  • ❌ Faster forgetting
  • Best for: Exact recall tasks

Paraphrase:

  • ✅ Memorization and semantic performance similar
  • ✅ More stable retention over time
  • ✅ Better compositional understanding
  • Best for: Robust knowledge acquisition

Finding 6: Forgetting Follows Logarithmic Decay

Forgetting follows a power-law relationship with respect to training steps:

R(t) ∝ 1/log(t)

Practical implications:

  • First 10 steps: ~23% probability loss
  • Next 100 steps: another ~23% loss
  • Next 1,000 steps: another ~23% loss

The forgetting rate is faster for duplicated content than paraphrased content.

Finding 7: Batch Size Reduces Forgetting

Increasing batch size reduces the slope of forgetting:

  • Larger batches → more stable gradients → slower forgetting
  • But doesn’t eliminate the fundamental forgetting problem

Implications for Real-World Applications

The Long-Tail Knowledge Problem

Definition: Long-tail entities are facts that appear infrequently in training data.

The Problem:

dP(fact)/dt = α·exposure(t) - β·P(fact)

Where:

  • α = effectivity (higher for larger models)
  • β = forgetting rate (roughly constant)
  • exposure(t) = 1 when fact is in batch, 0 otherwise

For long-tail facts:

  • exposure(t) ≈ single delta function (rare spike)
  • Probability briefly increases, then decays
  • By end of training: P(fact) ≈ 0

Connection to Latin American Cultural Knowledge

Reference: Karmim et al., “Leveraging Wikidata for Geographically Informed Sociocultural Bias Dataset Creation: Application to Latin America” (EACL 2026 @ Workshop MME)

Empirical validation of long-tail problem:

  • Large models underperform on Latin American cultural knowledge
  • Despite Wikipedia coverage, these facts are rarely encountered during training
  • Performance metrics:
    • Llama 3.1-8B: 65.9% (Portuguese)
    • GPT-4: 80.0% (English)
    • Mistral-large: 84.3% (Portuguese)

The Learnability Threshold

Key insight: If encounters are too far apart, forgetting completely erases previous acquisition.

From Chang et al., the x-intercept (complete forgetting) occurs around 10^11 tokens.

Implication: Facts appearing once in 2T tokens are effectively unlearnable.

The Scientific Bottleneck

Three major challenges prevent effective knowledge acquisition in LLMs:

Challenge 1: Long-Tail Knowledge Acquisition

Key papers:

  • Mallen et al. (ACL 2023): “When Not to Trust Language Models”
  • Feldman (STOC 2020): “Does Learning Require Memorization?”
  • Kandpal et al. (ICML 2023): “Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge”

Core problem:

  • LLMs struggle with rare entities regardless of model size
  • Larger models partially compensate via implicit upsampling
  • Unknown extent in frontier models (GPT-4, Claude, etc.)

Challenge 2: Fine-Tuning Risks

Key papers:

  • Luo et al. (2024): “New knowledge injection causes hallucinations”
  • Gekhman et al. (EMNLP 2024): “Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?”
  • Ovadia et al. (EMNLP 2024): “Fine-Tuning Can Cripple Your Foundation Model”

Core problems:

  • Adding new knowledge during fine-tuning → increased hallucinations
  • Catastrophic forgetting during continual fine-tuning
  • Trade-off between new knowledge and existing capabilities

Challenge 3: RAG Superiority

Key papers:

  • Soudani et al. (SIGIR 2024): “Retrieval-Augmented Generation”
  • Ovadia et al. (EMNLP 2024): “RAG vs Fine-Tuning comparison”

Core findings:

  • External databases consistently outperform parametric memory
  • Especially effective for long-tail entities
  • More reliable and updatable than fine-tuning

Future Directions: Knowledge Graph Integration

Three promising approaches to address these challenges:

Approach 1: KG-RAG Methods (G-Retriever)

Key features:

  • Curated knowledge from trusted sources (Wikidata, DBpedia)
  • Multi-hop reasoning capabilities
  • Strict relation/concept/hierarchy definitions

Advantages:

  • Verifiable facts
  • Explainable reasoning paths
  • Easy to update

Approach 2: KG During Training

Reference: Chen et al. (ICLR 2025)

Pipeline:

  1. Extractor: Named entity recognition from training text
  2. Generator: Extract reasoning subgraphs from KG
  3. Detector: Identify knowledge conflicts
  4. Integration: Combine text + KG during pretraining

Benefits:

  • Structured knowledge from the start
  • Conflict detection and resolution
  • Better fact grounding

Approach 3: Architectural Integration (KnowBERT)

Reference: Peters et al., “Knowledge Enhanced Contextual Word Representations”

Key innovations:

  • Specific attention heads dedicated to KG
  • Explicit knowledge graph completion learning
  • Entity linking integrated into architecture

Architecture components:

  1. Standard transformer layers
  2. KG integration layers
  3. Entity linking modules
  4. Knowledge attention heads

Conclusion

Key Takeaways

  1. Knowledge acquisition is incremental: LLMs learn through small probability accumulations, not sudden insights

  2. Forgetting is immediate and logarithmic: Knowledge degrades quickly after acquisition, following power-law decay

  3. Long-tail knowledge remains challenging: Rare facts are nearly impossible to learn reliably through pretraining alone

  4. More data ≠ better learning: Training stage doesn’t improve learning capability for new facts

  5. Model size helps, but isn’t enough: Larger models have better effectivity, but still face fundamental forgetting

  6. Paraphrase > duplication: Varied exposures lead to more robust, stable knowledge

The Path Forward

Current evidence suggests:

  • Parametric knowledge storage has fundamental limitations
  • RAG/external databases more reliable for factual knowledge
  • Knowledge graphs offer structured, verifiable alternative
  • Hybrid approaches most promising: combining parametric reasoning with non-parametric knowledge retrieval

Final Thoughts

The research by Chang et al. fundamentally challenges our understanding of how LLMs “know” things. Rather than true knowledge acquisition, pretraining may be better understood as statistical pattern matching with severe limitations for rare information.

For practical applications requiring factual accuracy:

  • Prefer RAG over fine-tuning for new knowledge
  • Use knowledge graphs for structured, verifiable facts
  • Accept parametric limitations and build hybrid systems
  • Focus on retrieval quality over model size alone

References

Primary Paper

  • Chang, T. Y., et al. (2024). “How do Large Language Models Acquire Factual Knowledge During Pretraining?” NeurIPS 2024.

Long-Tail Knowledge

  • Mallen, A., et al. (2023). “When Not to Trust Language Models: Investigating Effectiveness of Parametric and Non-Parametric Memories.” ACL 2023.
  • Feldman, V. (2020). “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail.” STOC 2020.
  • Kandpal, N., et al. (2023). “Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge.” ICML 2023.

Fine-Tuning Risks

  • Luo, H., et al. (2024). “New Knowledge Injection Causes Hallucinations in Large Language Models.”
  • Gekhman, Z., et al. (2024). “Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?” EMNLP 2024.
  • Ovadia, O., et al. (2024). “Fine-Tuning Can Cripple Your Foundation Model; Preserving Features May be the Solution.” EMNLP 2024.

RAG and Knowledge Graphs

  • Soudani, H., et al. (2024). “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for AI-Generated Content: A Survey.” SIGIR 2024.
  • Chen, Y., et al. (2025). “Knowledge Graph Integration During Pretraining.” ICLR 2025.
  • Peters, M., et al. “Knowledge Enhanced Contextual Word Representations.”

Related Work

  • Karmim, Y., et al. (2026). “Leveraging Wikidata for Geographically Informed Sociocultural Bias Dataset Creation: Application to Latin America.” EACL 2026 Workshop on Multilingual Multicultural Evaluation (MME).

About This Research

This blog post synthesizes research presented in my talk at INRIA Chile (March 2026). For questions or collaboration opportunities, feel free to reach out.

entry.title: Expressivity of GNNs
entry.content:
Graph Neural Networks are the state-of-the-art models for representation learning on graphs. Message-passing architectures have become dominant in this field thanks to their simplicity and their performance on graph tasks.

However, unlike their cousins in the neural-network family (CNNs, MLPs, Transformers), their expressivity is bounded by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. In this post we first look at what the Weisfeiler-Lehman algorithm is, and why understanding it is essential to design better models and go beyond the limits of standard GNN architectures.

We then look at how recent GNN models manage to exceed the expressivity bound of the 1-WL test, and finally we discuss the expressivity of GNNs on dynamic graphs, a field that is still very little studied.

Expressivity and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test

The 1-WL test

The following figures are borrowed from M. Bronstein’s blog post on the expressivity of GNNs

The 1-WL test is a polynomial-time algorithm designed by Weisfeiler and Lehman in 1968 to determine whether two graphs are isomorphic. Two graphs are isomorphic when their structures are identical.

The test iteratively recolors the nodes of a graph.

For each node, we aggregate the colors of its neighborhood and recolor the current node with an injective hash function. We repeat this process until convergence (the color of each node no longer changes from one iteration to the next).

If two graphs are isomorphic, their colorings will be identical at the end of the process.

This algorithm distinguishes graph structures in almost all situations, with some exceptions such as regular graphs.

The WL test is based on iterative graph recoloring (a “color” in graph theory is a discrete node label), starting with all nodes having the same color. At each step, the algorithm aggregates the colors of nodes and their neighborhoods, represents them as multisets, and hashes the aggregated color multisets into new unique colors. The algorithm stops when it reaches a stable coloring. If at that point the colorings of the two graphs differ, the graphs are deemed non-isomorphic. If the colorings are the same, the graphs are possibly (but not necessarily) isomorphic. In other words, the WL test is a necessary but insufficient condition for graph isomorphism. There exist non-isomorphic graphs for which the WL test produces identical colorings and considers them “possibly isomorphic”; the test is said to fail in this case. Such an example is shown in the following figure:

How Powerful are GNNs? (2018)

How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks? showed that standard message-passing architectures (GCN, GAT, SAGE) are bounded in expressivity by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test; moreover, in most cases these GNNs are much weaker than the 1-WL test at telling graph structures apart.

Being bounded means that graph structures that this test cannot distinguish cannot be distinguished by MP-GNNs either. In the paper, the authors then designed the most expressive MP-GNN, matching the 1-WL test: the GIN model.

For an architecture to be as expressive as the 1-WL test, some conditions must hold on the neighborhood aggregation and on the readout function.

The readout function aggregates all node embeddings to produce a representation of the whole graph.

An expressive GNN must never represent two different neighborhoods the same way, so we need an injective neighborhood aggregation function. The same holds for the readout function that produces the global graph representation.

The goal is the following:

\[\text{Let } G_{1} \text{ and } G_{2} \text{ be two non-isomorphic graphs; a GNN } \mathcal{A}: \mathcal{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d} \text{ should represent } G_{1} \text{ and } G_{2} \text{ differently,}\]

whenever the Weisfeiler-Lehman test also determines that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are not isomorphic.

The authors introduce the following theorem. Let $\mathcal{A}: \mathcal{G} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a GNN. For any two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ that the WL test declares non-isomorphic, $\mathcal{A}$ maps them to different representations if the following conditions hold:

a) $\mathcal{A}$ aggregates and updates node representations as

\[h_{v}^{(k)} = \phi\left(h_{v}^{(k-1)}, f\left(\{ h_{u}^{(k-1)} : u \in \mathcal{N}(v) \}\right)\right)\]

where the functions $f$ (operating on multisets) and $\phi$ are injective;

b) the readout function, operating on the multiset of node representations, is injective.

Going beyond the 1-WL test

The k-WL test

Recent research on GNNs has tried to exceed the expressivity bound of the 1-WL test.

The 1-WL test is limited and cannot capture simple graph structures such as closed triangles or cycles (Can Graph Neural Networks Count Substructures?).

The WL test can be generalized into a hierarchy of higher-order tests, known as the k-WL tests. This hierarchy has been used to characterize the expressive power of GNNs and to inspire the design of new GNN architectures.

In the k-WL algorithm (k > 1), we no longer color a node but a k-tuple of nodes.

For example, the 2-WL test no longer considers a node and its neighborhood but a pair of nodes. Instead of aggregating the colors of neighboring nodes (1-WL case), it aggregates the colors of neighboring triangles.

This lets the test describe more complex patterns, and so exceed the expressivity of the 1-WL test.

In the example above, the 1-WL test concludes the graphs are isomorphic, while the 3-WL test distinguishes them.

Although more expressive, the k-WL test is far more expensive, since it considers every k-tuple of nodes in the graph, including non-adjacent ones.

The video below helps understand the WL test and visualize the higher-dimensional cases.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YHeeAB_XRS4&list=PLeKJtN5YzWyPoNyqL34y5Jrag7aqgQRn5&index=10

A full playlist on graph isomorphism, the Weisfeiler-Lehman algorithm and graph transformers is available here.

  • Further resources on the WL algorithm and its adaptations in machine learning:
    • Weisfeiler and Leman go Machine Learning: The Story so far
    • A survey on the expressive power of graph neural networks
    • A Short Tutorial on The Weisfeiler-Lehman Test And Its Variants

k-GNNs

Contributions such as Weisfeiler and Leman Go Neural: Higher-order Graph Neural Networks or Provably Powerful Graph Networks design k-GNNs based on the k-WL test and reach the same theoretical expressivity. However, these techniques have a high memory and time complexity and are often impractical on large graphs.

Subgraph-based GNNs

Decomposing a graph into several subgraphs processed by a GNN greatly improves model expressivity. Bouritsas et al. present a fast method that is more expressive than the 1-WL test: Improving Graph Neural Network Expressivity via Subgraph Isomorphism Counting (ICLR 2021).

A note on this paper is detailed in this post by M. Bronstein:

Beyond Weisfeiler-Lehman: using substructures for provably expressive graph neural networks

The idea is to treat messages differently, and explicitly, depending on the local structure of the graph. Messages go through additional functions describing the structure associated with each node, so messages coming from different structures are not aggregated the same way. This requires counting certain substructures; choosing these substructures injects an inductive bias that can greatly improve learning on some tasks (e.g. counting closed triangles in a social network, or cycles in protein interactions).

Their model GSN (Graph Substructure Networks) theoretically exceeds the expressivity of the 1-WL test while keeping locality and the same complexity (during training) as message-passing architectures, unlike the k-GNN methods discussed above.

Method:

The core of GSN is a preprocessing step that builds node features encoding predefined substructures of the graph $G$.

We first define a set of structures we want to identify in the graph:

$\mathcal{H} = {H_{1},H_{2},…,H_{k}}$

The set $\mathcal{H}$ contains substructures such as a 3-clique or a cycle of a given length.

For each $H$, we find the set of its isomorphic subgraphs in $G$, denoted $G_{S}$.

For each node $v \in V_{G_{S}}$, we infer its role in $H$ by getting the orbit of its mapping $f(v)$ in $H$, $Orb_{H}(f(v))$. By counting all possible appearances of the different orbits at $v$, we obtain the structural feature of $v$, $\mathbf{x}_{H}^{V}$.

The worst-case complexity of this preprocessing is $\mathcal{O}(n^{k})$, with $k$ the size of the substructures in $\mathcal{H}$.

In the figure (left part), the neighborhood of the current node (blue) contains a 3-cycle (red), a 4-node pattern (yellow) and three paths of length 3.

The right part of the figure follows the same principle, targeting an edge instead of a node.

Message passing is defined as follows:

$M^{t+1}$ is a message-aggregation function (MLP, attention…) and $UP^{t+1}$ is the update function of the current node representation.

These are the same operations as in a standard MP-GNN. The two variants GSN-e and GSN-v count substructures around a target edge and around a target node, respectively.

GSN is a message-passing GNN augmented with precomputed features that encode substructures in the local neighborhood of a node or an edge.

The choice of substructures is crucial for the model to generalize well. Good prior knowledge of the graph distribution matters (for instance, favoring graphlets for protein interactions, and cliques and triangles for social networks). How to choose the substructures remains an open question.

A large part of the paper is devoted to GSN’s expressivity: the authors prove that GSN is at least as expressive as the 1-WL test, and that, depending on the chosen substructures, it can reach the expressivity of the k-WL test.

Since GSN

Based on M. Bronstein’s blog post:

Using subgraphs for more expressive GNNs

GSN led to many contributions in the field of subgraph-based GNNs.

Dropout

It has been shown that subgraphs can be exploited to increase GNN expressivity through dropout, as in DropGNN (NeurIPS 2021) or DropEdge (ICLR 2020). By randomly removing nodes from the graph during message passing, and repeating this dropout a number of times, we obtain several subgraph embeddings around a node.

This method does not require selecting substructures beforehand.

GNNs and reconstruction

Reconstruction for Powerful Graph Representations (NeurIPS 2021) is based on the graph reconstruction conjecture.

Informally, the reconstruction conjecture in graph theory says that graphs are uniquely determined by their subgraphs.

The k-reconstruction GNNs proposed in this paper apply an MP-GNN to each induced subgraph of size k and sum the resulting embeddings. Since there can be too many such subgraphs, sampling is needed (similar to dropout GNNs).

From stars to subgraphs

From Stars to Subgraphs: Uplifting Any GNN with Local Structure Awareness (ICLR 2022)

In MP-GNNs and in 1-WL, aggregation follows a star pattern. To extend this limited representation, Zhao et al. use rooted subgraphs.

Besides capturing neighborhood information like the star pattern (left), rooted subgraphs also capture its connectivity (right).

This way of aggregating a node’s neighborhood is called subgraph-1-WL. The paper shows it is strictly more expressive than 1-WL and that it can distinguish some graphs that 3-WL cannot.

Subgraph-1-WL GNNs encode every subgraph with an MP-GNN.

Compared with dropout and reconstruction architectures, this method has the advantage of aggregating subgraphs that involve the same node several times.

Equivariant subgraphs

Equivariant Subgraph Aggregation Networks, ESAN (ICLR 2022)

Rather than encoding multisets of nodes as in 1-WL or MP-GNNs, they propose to encode a multiset of subgraphs.

To build these multisets of subgraphs, they propose four selection policies:

  • node deletion
  • edge deletion
  • two variants of ego-subgraphs (see the previous paragraph).

Their model is an equivariant framework to generate and process these subgraphs.

Why equivariant?

From the input graph (left), edge deletion can generate 3 subgraphs (middle), which leads to 3 different tensor representations, even though they are only permutations of the same subgraph pattern.

The equivariant framework aims to produce the same representation for each of these three using symmetry groups. ESAN builds on the work of Maron et al. (learning symmetric patterns).

ESAN has two encoders (orange and yellow): the first encodes the subgraph structures in parallel with a Siamese network; the second, information sharing, aggregates (sums) the representation tensors of the different subgraphs. The orange encoder generalizes dropout- or reconstruction-style models, and the information-sharing module generalizes the stars-to-subgraphs approach.

A key challenge for all these subgraph architectures is sampling: the space of subgraphs around a target node is often extremely large. So we must either predefine the structures (which requires prior knowledge of the graph distribution) or sample the subgraph structures (more or less cleverly).

More recently (2022)

Among architectures more expressive than 1-WL, subgraph GNNs are the biggest trend. Several approaches stand out:

1️⃣ Subgraph Union Networks (SUN) by Frasca, Bevilacqua, et al. provide a full analysis of the design space and expressivity of subgraph GNNs, showing they are bounded by the 3-WL test.

2️⃣ Ordered Subgraph Aggregation Networks (OSAN) by Qian, Rattan, et al. design a hierarchy of subgraph-enhanced GNNs (k-OSAN) and find that k-OSANs are incomparable to k-WL but strictly bounded by (k+1)-WL. A particularly cool part of OSAN is the use of Implicit MLE (NeurIPS’21), a differentiable discrete sampling technique, to sample the ordered subgraphs.

3️⃣ SpeqNets by Morris et al. design a permutation-equivariant hierarchy of graph networks that balances scalability and expressivity.

4️⃣ GraphSNN by Wijesinghe and Wang derive expressive models from the overlap between subgraph isomorphisms and subtree isomorphisms.

Expressivity of dynamic GNNs

Provably Expressive Temporal Graph Networks (NeurIPS 2022)

Context

This paper studies the expressivity of TGNs (Temporal Graph Networks) by grouping them into two families: TGNs that aggregate temporal random walks, WA-TGN (CAW), and models built on message passing, MP-TGN (TGN, TGAT, JODIE…). In both cases the paper considers continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDG); discrete-time graphs (DTDG) can be directly converted into CTDGs.

Reminder: state-of-the-art TGN architectures on CTDGs

MP-TGN family:

  • Know-Evolve / temporal point processes: approaches based on temporal point processes (TPP), parameterized by a neural network (RNN).
  • JODIE: an RNN approach where nodes are updated with a time-series model. In the bipartite case, two RNNs are used (users and items). A temporal projection updates a node’s memory; if a node has not been involved in any event for some time, its memory is considered stale.
  • TGAT: the first architecture to use time embeddings. During message aggregation, a time embedding (Time2Vec) represents the time elapsed between the present time t and the last interaction with the neighbor. The aggregation function is similar to GAT (attention weights over neighbors). The aggregated GNN layers Z(t) are then linearly projected into queries, keys and values, as in transformers.
  • TGN: a generic message-passing framework. On top of TGAT, TGN-attn uses a memory module for message passing and node updates, and also uses Time2Vec during message aggregation.

WA-TGN family:

  • CAW-N: generates anonymous (important for the model to be inductive) and causal random walks. Starting from a target edge (u, v), it samples random walks to find the nodes responsible for creating this link. The walks are encoded with an RNN, which forms the representation of the link only.

The goal of this work is to extend the study of static GNN expressivity (GIN, How Powerful are GNNs?, links to WL-based algorithms…) to temporal graphs, by defining a temporal 1-WL test.

After studying the expressivity of temporal GNNs, the authors propose a new architecture, PINT. Using injective temporal message passing and relative positional features, they show large gains over existing architectures while matching the expressivity of the temporal 1-WL test.

Isomorphism in temporal graphs

The expressivity of TGNs is evaluated by their ability to tell apart non-isomorphic structures in the graph. Two nodes that do not share the same local structure, or did not connect to their neighborhood at the same time $t$, should not get the same representation.

To measure the expressivity of an MP-TGN, we evaluate its ability to map two distinct nodes to different points of the embedding space:

$u\text{ and } v \text{ are different, so } h_{u}^{(L)}(t) \neq h_{v}^{(L)}(t).$

The computation of a node $v$’s representation at time $t$ can be described with a TCT (Temporal Computation Tree), denoted $T_{v}(t)$.

The TCT is a computation tree induced from a source node.

On the left is a temporal graph: colors are node features, and $t_{1},t_{2}$ are the times at which nodes connect. On the right are the depth-2 TCTs of nodes $u$ and $v$.

If an MP-TGN of depth $L$ gives different representations to $u$ and $v$, then $T_{u}(t)$ and $T_{v}(t)$ are not isomorphic.

In the example above, models such as TGN-attn or TGAT cannot distinguish $T_{u}(t)$ from $T_{v}(t)$. Both use the mean of messages as aggregation function; since the proportion of features is the same in both cases, both models give $u$ and $v$ the same representation.

Simple structures such as cycles or cliques cannot be modeled by current MP-TGNs or WA-TGNs, even when the MP-TGN is as expressive as the temporal 1-WL test.

The paper also discusses MP-TGNs with a memory module, showing that if the TCT depth is smaller than the number of layers $L$, the memory module does not improve the model’s expressivity.

Extending 1-WL to the temporal case

1-WL is an isomorphism test on static graphs based on iterative node recoloring: at the end of the process, if two graphs have the same coloring, they are (possibly) isomorphic.

This algorithm extends to temporal graphs by viewing the dynamic graph as a multigraph (several links possible between two nodes).

The PINT model

The authors present PINT (position-encoding injective temporal graph net). The model has two components:

  1. Injective message aggregation and representation updates in a temporal setting.
  2. Positional features generated from the TCTs.

Injective aggregation

As in GIN, the best way to maximize the expressivity of MP-TGNs is to use injective aggregation functions. On dynamic graphs, it matters when links were created between two nodes. A common inductive bias is to give more weight to recent events (TGN, TGAT).

\[\tilde{h}_v^{(\ell)}(t)=\sum_{\left(u, e, t^{\prime}\right) \in \mathcal{N}(v, t)} \operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{agg}}^{(\ell)}\left(h_u^{(\ell-1)}(t) \| e\right) \alpha^{-\beta\left(t-t^{\prime}\right)}\]

As injective functions they use MLPs, as in GIN (universal approximators of continuous functions).

To give more weight to recent events, PINT uses an exponential time decay, $\alpha^{-\beta(t-t^{‘})}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are hyperparameters.

\[h_v^{(\ell)}(t)=\operatorname{MLP}_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(\ell)}\left(h_v^{(\ell-1)}(t) \| \tilde{h}_v^{(\ell)}(t)\right)\]

The update function must also be injective to maximize expressivity; $|$ denotes vector concatenation, and $h_{v}^{(0)} = s_{v}(t)$ is the state vector of node $v$.

Relative positional features

The authors propose to augment the state vector $s$ of each node with relative positional features.

The idea is to count how many temporal walks of a given length exist between two nodes (how many times nodes appear at different levels of the TCT).

We consider a square matrix $P$; each row gives the relative position of every node with respect to the target node.

PINT with positional features is strictly more expressive than WA-TGNs and MP-TGNs.

Limits of PINT

PINT is bounded by the temporal 1-WL test: any non-isomorphic structures that T-1-WL deems isomorphic cannot be distinguished by PINT either.

Because of the symmetry of this graph, PINT cannot give different representations to these two events. So there is still room to improve the expressivity of TGN models.

Results

The experimental protocol used here is the same as in TGN, TGAT, CAW… It would be interesting to evaluate PINT with the new protocol introduced at NeurIPS 2022, Towards Better Evaluation for Dynamic Link Prediction.
entry.summary: A note on the expressive power of static and dynamic graph neural networks, from the Weisfeiler-Lehman test to subgraph GNNs and temporal graph networks.
